audit.action: check whether this is the same language as another entry
audit.recode_to: Retire the kala1380 'Bulloo River' record (or re-key it to ngur1261 and merge with the existing 'Wangkumara' record). M&W 1979 describe 'Wangkumara (Galali)', a Wilson River dialect, and state on p.1 that it is 'clearly different' from Breen's Bulloo River Galali (= Glottolog kala1380 with dialects Kalali/Pitjara/Mingbari). After the merge, reconcile the two rule strings drawn from the same sentence: kala1380 carries stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (connected-speech reading, finals unstressed) while ngur1261 carries StressTyp2's alternating stress from the left (citation-form reading); the ngur1261 record's own corr note already says three of four survey channels favour the no-final-stress variant. No stress source is known for kala1380 proper, so that languoid should drop out of the catalog (no-stress-source-exists) unless Breen's Kalali MSS say otherwise.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim at M&W 1979 sec. 2.1 p.5 (p.15) in the copy consulted; the record's 'held' field is empty only because the file is stored under ngur1261. (2) Source: a 1979 Pacific Linguistics 'basic materials' sketch from one speaker's 1963 tapes; adequate for the lect it describes, and the only published stress statement for it. (3) Identity: the book's Introduction explicitly distinguishes its 'Wangkumara (Galali)' (Wilson River language, Glottolog ngur1261) from Breen's Bulloo River Galali/Pitjara/Minkabari (= Glottolog kala1380's dialect set). sources.citation: McDonald & Wurm 1979, Basic Materials in Wankumara (Galali), PL B-65 sec. 2.1, full PDF via sealang.net; caveats: 'normally', emphasis shifts stress, 2-syllable suffixes take secondary stress
sources.quote: Primary stress occurs normally on the first syllable of a word, with secondary stress on third and fifth syllables - except that final syllables are unstressed in connected speech.
